In Rwanda's parliament, women hold roughly 64% of the seats — the highest share on Earth, and not close. The global average is about 27%.

One map, and the reason traces back to one of the darkest chapters in modern history — a thread 🧵🗺️

Data: Our World in Data (CC BY)

1/ The map shows the share of seats in the lower house held by women. Rwanda's dark purple isn't a rounding fluke — it's held the world's #1 spot for two decades, ahead of Cuba, Nicaragua, Mexico, and every Nordic country.

2/ The story starts in 1994. The genocide killed an estimated 500,000–800,000 people, overwhelmingly men. Some estimates put the post-genocide population at 60–70% female. Rebuilding a state meant putting women into roles men had filled.

3/ Rwanda's 2003 constitution set a floor, not a ceiling: at least 30% of seats in every decision-making body, national and local, reserved for women. It was meant as a minimum. Rwanda blew past it and kept climbing toward 64%.

4/ Compare the map's other end: Yemen sits near 0%, and several Gulf states aren't far off. The ~27% global average is dragged down less by any single region than by dozens of countries with no quota system at all.

5/ Quotas alone don't guarantee this outcome — plenty of countries with quotas hover right at their legal floor. Rwanda's outlier status also reflects a ruling party that made women's inclusion central to its post-genocide legitimacy.

6/ The map's next-darkest cluster — Mexico, Bolivia, Australia, the Nordics — got there by different routes: legislated candidate parity, proportional representation that makes quotas easy to enforce, and decades of gradual reform.
